advisor.summary: An SSTB owner above the §199A threshold loses the deduction on specified-service income, but the fence is drawn activity by activity: practice-owned real estate, product lines, and service operations with genuine outside customers are not specified services and can hold or recover QBI status in their own entities. The final regulations killed the paper version — under Reg. §1.199A-5(c)(2), a 50%-commonly-owned entity providing 80% or more of its property or services to the SSTB is treated as part of the SSTB, with pro-rata taint below 80%. What survives is separation with substance: real employees, arm's-length contracts, and meaningful third-party revenue. Advisory-only, because the value turns on facts — revenue mix, pricing, operational substance — that cannot be computed honestly from return inputs.
mechanics: SSTB status attaches to each trade or business separately under the field definitions of Reg. §1.199A-5(b) — a medical practice is a specified service, but its building, a device or products line, an imaging operation, or a billing company serving many practices need not be.

The anti-abuse rule of Reg. §1.199A-5(c)(2): with 50%-or-greater common ownership (attribution applies), a separated entity providing at least 80% of its property or services to the SSTB is treated entirely as part of the SSTB; below 80%, the SSTB-serving portion is tainted pro rata.

The reverse trap in Reg. §1.199A-5(c)(1): a business with gross receipts of $25 million or less is wholly an SSTB if more than 10% of receipts come from specified services (5% above $25 million) — keep professional-service revenue out of the clean entity entirely.

Self-rental can serve the structure: rental to a commonly controlled pass-through is a §199A trade or business under Reg. §1.199A-1(b)(14), but rental income from a commonly owned SSTB tenant is itself treated as SSTB income — outside or non-SSTB tenants keep rental QBI clean.

Substance carries the structure: the separated entity needs its own employees, contracts, market pricing, books, and licenses, or it invites §482 reallocation and the separate-entity baseline of Moline Properties.
Composition: once separated, the clean non-SSTB entities can layer W-2 wage optimization and aggregation under Reg. §1.199A-4 among themselves — an SSTB can never aggregate with anything.

authority.note: The SSTB definition — the fence this structuring works around; non-SSTB activities sit outside it even under common ownership.
The anti-crack-and-pack rule: a 50%-commonly-owned entity providing 80% or more of its property or services to the SSTB is treated as part of it; below 80%, tainted pro rata.
The de minimis rule: more than 10% of gross receipts from specified services (5% above $25M) taints the entire business as an SSTB.
The field-by-field map of specified services — what can and cannot be separated cleanly.
Self-rental to a commonly controlled pass-through is a §199A trade or business — the hook that gives separated real estate QBI status, subject to the SSTB-tenant taint.
The aggregation rules the clean entities can use among themselves after separation.
IRS authority to reallocate income among commonly controlled entities where intercompany pricing is not arm's length.

authority.cite: Moline Properties, Inc. v. Commissioner, 319 U.S. 436 (1943)
authority.note: A separate entity is respected only if it carries on actual business activity — the substance floor every spun-off entity must clear.

requirements: A genuinely separable non-SSTB activity — owned real estate, products, equipment, or services — with real or realistically attainable third-party customers.
Either meaningful outside revenue keeping the entity under the 80% test, or common ownership below 50% after attribution.
Full operational substance in the separated entity: employees, intercompany contracts at market pricing, separate books, accounts, licenses, and insurance.
Professional-service receipts in the clean entity held below the 10% (or 5%) de minimis line.
risks: Recharacterization under Reg. §1.199A-5(c)(2) is the leading theory: a captive entity serving mostly the commonly owned SSTB is simply treated as the SSTB, so the structure buys nothing but cost — the regulation is the controlling authority, written specifically to kill this fact pattern.
Off-market intercompany pricing draws §482 reallocation; management fees and rents set to move income rather than reflect value are the classic finding.

A spun-off entity with no employees or independent activity fails the baseline of Moline Properties, Inc. v. Commissioner, 319 U.S. 436 (1943) — separate existence is respected only with actual business activity.
The recovered deduction must clear a real annual hurdle: separate returns, payroll, insurance, licensing, and intercompany accounting.
Each new entity multiplies state consequences — franchise tax, nexus, and PTET eligibility all fragment.
stateNotes: Conformity: §199A is a federal below-AGI deduction most states never conform to, so the state benefit of the structure is usually zero — the state case rests on liability protection and operations, not tax.

PTET: restructuring changes which entities can elect a pass-through entity tax and how the PTET deduction allocates, and PTET paid also reduces the QBI the structure is trying to protect — sequence the modeling.

Missouri: Missouri's own business income deduction (RSMo §143.022) is computed without the federal SSTB limitation, so Missouri-side value does not depend on this structuring; a restructured group re-evaluates SALT Parity Act PTET elections (RSMo §143.436) entity by entity.
reviewChecklist: The 80%/50% and de minimis tests are modeled on realistic revenue projections, not aspirations.
The outside-revenue plan is credible; if the separated entity cannot win third-party business, the recommendation is to stop.
Transfer-pricing support exists for every intercompany charge.
Substance checklist complete: employees, books, accounts, licenses, insurance.
Annual re-test calendared — revenue-mix drift can re-taint the structure.
State fragmentation (nexus, franchise, PTET) costed into the net benefit.

client.teaser: Parts of your business may still qualify for the 20% deduction — if they stand on their own.
client.headline: Separate what qualifies, and win back part of the 20% deduction
plainEnglish: For certain professions, the 20% business deduction goes away at higher incomes. But the rule targets the professional work itself, not everything the business does. The building you own, products you sell, or services sold to other companies can still qualify.

When everything sits in one company, the tax law paints it all the same color. Move the qualifying pieces into their own real companies — with their own staff, contracts, and customers — and each piece gets judged on its own.

The word that matters is real. The IRS wrote rules against paper spin-offs. A new entity that only serves your practice changes nothing. We design structures with true substance, and we tell you honestly if yours will not clear the bar.
client.analogy: Think of one house where a single smoker gets the whole place labeled a smoking zone. Give the other activities their own buildings, and each is judged on its own air.
benefits: Recovers the 20% deduction on income that can qualify
Often adds liability protection and cleaner books
Creates building blocks for other strategies later
steps: WE inventory everything your business does and earns.
WE test which pieces can truly qualify on their own — and say so if none can.
WE design the entities, contracts, and pricing to meet the rules.
YOU run the new entities as real businesses — staff, invoices, separate accounts.
clientCommitments: Treat each entity as a real business — its own account, records, and contracts
Grow genuine outside revenue in the separated companies
Accept the ongoing cost of extra returns and bookkeeping

annualMaintenance: Annual re-test of the 80% and de minimis revenue mixes
Entity-by-entity PTET and state filing review
deliverables: Structuring memo with the 80%/50% and de minimis analysis
